title: Tissue Allografts Without Matching: Heart Valves and Corneas
summary: Learn why corneas and cardiac valve homografts are transplanted without routine HLA matching, where corneal immune privilege fails, why valve homografts still sensitise recipients, and how donor corneas are stored.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 43 Hit 2 (cardiac valve allografts), Hit 3 (cornea) and Traps 1–2, checked against Olejkowska 2024, Armitage 2019, Böhringer 2018 (FANCY; read via a page-fetch tool), Pels 2008, Jahnukainen 2019, Huyan 2021 and Baskett 2003 (abstract only). Qualifications: the reviewer’s “valves need NO ABO/HLA matching … nonviable connective tissue” is qualified by sources showing cryopreserved homografts keep living, HLA-bearing cells and that ABO and HLA-DR mismatch were associated with faster failure in children (register flag rv-valve-homograft-matching); the reviewer’s corneal timings (enucleation within 6 h, 4 °C, transplant within 48–72 h) reflect older practice — modern cold storage is used for about 7–10 days and organ culture up to 4–5 weeks (rv-cornea-storage-times); the reviewer’s “~10% rejected, mostly from vascularization” and “>90% long-term success” are qualified by 20–30% rejection within 5 years and several independent risk factors (rv-cornea-rejection-risk). Not taught: ABO matching for corneas, donor age limits, US transplant counts.

objectives: Explain the anatomical, cellular and molecular barriers that make the cornea immunologically privileged, and the factors that break that privilege.
Explain why cryopreserved valve homografts are implanted without HLA matching yet can sensitise recipients, and why this matters for a later heart transplant.
Compare hypothermic and organ-culture storage of donor corneas.

scenes.title: Two grafts, one question
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a tissue bank receives two requests on the same day — (1) a 4-year-old with congenital heart disease who needs a cryopreserved pulmonary valve homograft to rebuild the right ventricular outflow tract; (2) an adult with keratoconus, first graft, who needs a donor cornea. A resident asks: “Do we HLA-type both, like a kidney?” A third token asks what happens if the child later needs a heart transplant.

cues.text: Two requests reach the tissue bank. A four-year-old needs a donor pulmonary valve, and an adult with keratoconus needs a donor cornea for a first graft.
The resident asks: do we HLA-type both of them, the way we would for a kidney?
And if the child needs a heart transplant years later, does that old valve matter?

props.label: Later heart transplant: does the valve matter?

scenes.title: Why these grafts skip routine matching
scenes.altText: Schematic split: left, a clear cornea with three labelled barriers of immune privilege — anatomical (no blood or lymphatic vessels in a healthy cornea), cellular (few mature antigen-presenting cells), molecular (FasL and PD-L1 on corneal cells, an immunosuppressive aqueous humour, and anterior chamber-associated immune deviation, ACAID). A token: HLA typing is not part of routine corneal eligibility. Right, a valve homograft card: usually implanted without HLA matching or immunosuppression (both are still research directions); in one paediatric series grafts were selected by ABO group only.

cues.text: The healthy cornea is immunologically privileged. Its first barrier is anatomy: no blood vessels and no lymphatic vessels, so immune cells have no easy route in or out.
It also has few mature antigen-presenting cells, and molecular brakes: Fas ligand and PD-L1 on corneal cells, an immunosuppressive aqueous humour, and anterior chamber-associated immune deviation.
That is why routine eligibility rules for corneal transplantation do not include HLA typing of donor and recipient.
Valve homografts are usually implanted without HLA matching or immunosuppression; both are still described as research directions. In one children’s series, grafts were chosen by ABO group only.

scenes.title: Where the privilege fails
scenes.altText: Left card, cornea risk (Australian Corneal Graft Registry data as summarised in a 2019 review): 4-year full-thickness graft survival 83% with no recipient neovascularisation vs 50% with 4-quadrant vessels; keratoconus first graft 95%, second 86%, third 71%; pretransplant inflammation and raised intraocular pressure also lower survival. High-risk recipients: rejection in 30–60%, up to 70% fail within 10 years. Even with steroid prophylaxis, 20–30% of corneal recipients have at least one rejection episode within 5 years. Right card, valves: cryopreservation keeps living donor cells, including endothelial and dendritic cells carrying HLA class II; most recipients make HLA antibodies (40–60% of children in earlier studies); the immune response is linked to early degeneration; in one paediatric series, ABO and HLA-DR mismatch were associated with faster echocardiographic valve failure.

cues.text: Privilege is relative. When vessels grow into the recipient cornea, graft survival falls: in registry data, four-year survival was eighty-three percent with no vessels, but fifty percent with vessels in all four quadrants.
Repeat grafts, inflammation and raised eye pressure also raise the risk. In high-risk eyes, rejection occurs in thirty to sixty percent, and up to seventy percent fail within ten years.
Valve homografts are not inert either. Cryopreservation keeps living donor cells, including endothelial and dendritic cells that carry HLA class two, and most recipients make HLA antibodies.
The immune response is linked to early valve degeneration, especially in children. In one paediatric series, ABO and HLA-DR mismatch were associated with faster valve failure.

props.title: Valve: not inert
lines: HLA class II on donor cells

scenes.title: What the lab and eye bank see
scenes.altText: Left card: a child with a valve homograft listed for heart transplant (one Finnish series of 12): 67% had HLA antibodies before transplant; after transplant 40% developed donor-specific antibodies against the homograft donor; in one child, homograft-donor antibodies were first detected 13.6 years after insertion. Decellularised grafts reduce sensitisation. Right card: corneal storage — hypothermic 2–6 °C, typically used for 7–10 days (media claim 14–16), death-to-storage usually 12 h or less; organ culture 31–37 °C, up to 4–5 weeks, death-to-storage 24–48 h; corneas cannot reliably be frozen. Bottom: hook answers.

cues.text: For the HLA lab, the valve matters later. In one series of children with homografts who needed heart transplants, two thirds already had HLA antibodies, and in one child, antibodies against the homograft donor were first detected more than thirteen years after surgery.

For the eye bank, storage sets the clock. Cold storage at two to six degrees is typically used for seven to ten days. Organ culture at thirty-one to thirty-seven degrees allows up to four to five weeks. Corneas cannot reliably be frozen.
Back to the hook. The cornea for a first keratoconus graft needs no routine HLA typing, and that is a low-risk graft.
The child’s valve is implanted without HLA matching, but record it: it may sensitise the child, which matters when the HLA lab screens for antibodies before a later heart transplant.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A valve homograft is inert dead scaffolding” (✓ cryopreserved valves keep living donor cells; most recipients make HLA antibodies); “HLA matching is proven to protect high-risk corneas” (✓ not proven: the randomised FANCY trial, in a mixed normal- and high-risk group, found no significant benefit — 2-year rejection 15.7% matched vs 17% control — but was underpowered; efficacy in high-risk grafts remains undetermined and some European centres still match); “Donor corneas must be used within 48–72 hours” (✓ that reflects older storage; modern cold media are used for about 7–10 days and organ culture up to 4–5 weeks).

cues.text: Trap one: a valve homograft is inert, dead scaffolding. No: cryopreserved valves keep living donor cells, and most recipients make HLA antibodies.

Trap two: HLA matching is proven to protect high-risk corneas. No: the randomised FANCY trial, in mixed normal- and high-risk patients, found no significant benefit, but it was underpowered, so the question remains open.
Trap three: a donor cornea must be used within forty-eight to seventy-two hours. No: modern cold storage is used for about a week or more, and organ culture for up to four weeks.

scenes.title: No roads in, tenants left behind
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The cornea is a village with NO ROADS — no vessels, so immune cells cannot drive in; build roads (neovascularisation) and the village is raided. A valve homograft is a house sold WITH TENANTS still inside — living donor cells that the recipient’s immune system notices and remembers.” Tokens: no roads = cornea · tenants = valve. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the cornea is a village with no roads. Without vessels, immune cells cannot drive in, but build roads and the village is raided. A valve homograft is a house sold with tenants still inside: living donor cells the immune system notices and remembers.

Where it breaks: corneal privilege also depends on molecular signals, not just missing vessels; decellularised valves remove most tenants; and whether HLA matching helps high-risk corneas is still unresolved.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Cornea: privileged, no routine HLA typing — but vessels, regrafts and inflammation raise rejection risk”, “Valve homograft: no matching, yet living donor cells sensitise — screen HLA antibodies before a later heart transplant”.

cues.text: Corneas and valve homografts are usually transplanted without HLA matching, but corneal privilege weakens in vascularised or regrafted eyes, and living donor cells in valves can sensitise recipients against HLA antigens that matter for a later heart transplant.

props.label: Cornea: no routine HLA typing · vessels/regraft = high risk
Valve: no matching · living cells sensitise → screen HLA antibodies

explanation.what: Plain language: most transplanted organs need careful tissue matching, but corneas and donor heart valves are usually given without it. The healthy cornea has no blood vessels, so the immune system rarely reaches it; donor valves still carry some living donor cells, which can make the recipient form antibodies. Scientific terms: immune privilege, neovascularisation, antigen-presenting cells, Fas ligand (FasL), PD-L1, anterior chamber-associated immune deviation (ACAID), keratoplasty, homograft (allograft) valved conduit, cryopreservation, decellularisation, HLA antibodies, donor-specific antibodies (DSA), hypothermic storage, organ culture.
explanation.why: The cornea’s lack of blood and lymphatic vessels, its few mature antigen-presenting cells and its local immunosuppressive signals limit sensitisation, so routine corneal eligibility rules do not include HLA typing. Valve homografts are usually implanted without HLA matching or immunosuppression (in one paediatric series they were selected by ABO group only), but cryopreservation preserves donor endothelial and dendritic cells that carry HLA, so recipients often make HLA antibodies.
explanation.measure: Cornea: 4-year full-thickness survival 83% with no recipient vessels vs 50% with 4-quadrant vessels (registry data); keratoconus first graft 95%, second 86%, third 71%; high-risk rejection 30–60%; 20–30% of all recipients have at least one rejection within 5 years. FANCY: 2-year rejection 15.7% matched vs 17% control (no significant difference; underpowered). Storage: hypothermic 2–6 °C, typically 7–10 days (claimed maximum 14–16), death-to-storage usually ≤12 h; organ culture 31–37 °C, up to 4–5 weeks, death-to-storage 24–48 h; corneas cannot reliably be frozen. Valves: 40–60% of children develop HLA antibodies after allograft implantation (earlier studies cited by Jahnukainen 2019).
explanation.differs: Cornea (avascular, privileged; risk rises with vessels, regraft, inflammation, raised IOP) vs valve homograft (implanted without matching but antigenic; sensitisation matters for later solid-organ transplant) vs solid organs (matching and immunosuppression routine). Hypothermic storage vs organ culture.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: which graft needs no routine HLA matching, which recipient factor raises corneal rejection risk, why a child with a homograft needs HLA antibody screening before heart transplant, and which storage method allows the longest corneal storage.

mnemonic.text: The cornea is a village with NO ROADS — no vessels, so immune cells cannot drive in; build roads (neovascularisation) and the village is raided. A valve homograft is a house sold WITH TENANTS still inside — living donor cells that the immune system notices and remembers.
mnemonic.explanation: Links corneal privilege to absent vessels and valve sensitisation to surviving donor cells.
mnemonic.limitation: Corneal privilege also depends on molecular signals (FasL, PD-L1, ACAID), not only on missing vessels; decellularised valves remove most donor cells; the value of HLA matching in high-risk corneas is unresolved.

analogyLimitations: Cornea and valve drawings are schematic.
Registry survival figures come from one country’s registry as summarised in a review; centres differ.
takeaway: Corneas and valve homografts are usually transplanted without HLA matching, but corneal privilege weakens in vascularised or regrafted eyes, and living donor cells in valves can sensitise recipients against HLA antigens that matter for a later heart transplant.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old who received a cryopreserved pulmonary valve homograft at age 2 is now listed for heart transplantation. Which laboratory concern does the homograft raise?

options.text: HLA antibodies from sensitisation by donor cells in the homograft
options.rationale: Correct. Cryopreserved homografts keep living HLA-bearing donor cells, and many recipients develop HLA antibodies that can complicate heart transplant matching.

options.text: None, because a valve homograft is inert connective tissue
options.rationale: Incorrect. Cryopreservation preserves endothelial and dendritic cells, and most recipients make HLA antibodies.

options.text: Antibodies can be ignored because they appear only in the first months after surgery
options.rationale: Incorrect. In one series, antibodies against the homograft donor were first detected 13.6 years after insertion.

options.text: Only an ABO antibody titre is needed before transplant
options.rationale: Incorrect. The concern is HLA sensitisation; HLA antibody screening and identification are needed.

questions.stem: Which recipient finding most clearly marks a corneal transplant as high risk for rejection?

options.text: Blood vessels grown into the recipient cornea
options.rationale: Correct. Neovascularisation removes the anatomical barrier; registry 4-year survival fell from 83% with no vessels to 50% with 4-quadrant vessels.
Incorrect. This is a low-risk indication, with about 95% 4-year survival for a first full-thickness graft in registry data.

options.text: A donor not HLA-matched to the recipient
options.rationale: Incorrect. The randomised FANCY trial found no significant benefit of HLA matching as a standard measure; mismatch is not the defining high-risk factor.

options.text: A donor cornea stored for 7 days in cold storage medium
options.rationale: Incorrect. About 7–10 days is the typical period for modern hypothermic storage.

questions.stem: An eye bank wants to store donor corneas for up to about four weeks. Which method allows this?

options.rationale: Correct. Organ culture allows storage for up to 4–5 weeks, with endothelial inspection after storage.
Incorrect. Cold storage is typically used for about 7–10 days; media claim a maximum of 14–16 days.

options.text: Freezing in liquid nitrogen with a cryoprotectant
options.rationale: Incorrect. Corneas cannot reliably be frozen.
Incorrect. The moist chamber stores the whole globe; storage is extended by removing the corneoscleral button, and the 4–5 week method is organ culture.

references.citation: Olejkowska N, Gorczyca I, Rękas M, Garley M. Immunopathology of Corneal Allograft Rejection and Donor-Specific Antibodies (DSAs) as Immunological Predictors of Corneal Transplant Failure. Cells. 2024;13(18):1532. doi:10.3390/cells13181532
references.usedFor: Eligibility rules for corneal transplantation do not include HLA typing or DSA testing; HLA matching not routinely used in keratoplasty; three barriers of corneal immune privilege (no blood or lymphatic vessels; few mature APCs; FasL, PD-L1, aqueous humour, ACAID); privilege abolished in high-risk patients.

references.citation: Armitage WJ, Goodchild C, Griffin MD, et al. High-risk Corneal Transplantation: Recent Developments and Future Possibilities. Transplantation. 2019;103(12):2468-2478. doi:10.1097/tp.0000000000002938
references.usedFor: Immune privilege of the anterior segment; high-risk rejection 30–60% and up to 70% failure within 10 years; ACGR 4-year survival by neovascularisation (83% vs 73/66/63/50%) and by graft number (95/86/71/56%); inflammation and raised IOP as risk factors; efficacy of HLA matching in high-risk grafts undetermined, CCTS negative, matching still used at some European centres.

references.citation: Böhringer D, Grotejohann B, Ihorst G, Reinshagen H, Spierings E, Reinhard T. Rejection Prophylaxis in Corneal Transplant. Dtsch Arztebl Int. 2018;115(15):259-265. doi:10.3238/arztebl.2018.0259
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool. FANCY randomised trial: 2-year rejection 15.7% (matched) vs 17% (control), SHR 0.97, no significant benefit; normal- and high-risk indications included; underpowered, so benefit in selected patients not excluded; 20–30% of corneal recipients have at least one rejection within 5 years; repeat keratoplasty raises rejection risk.

references.citation: Pels E, Beele H, Claerhout I. Eye bank issues: II. Preservation techniques: warm versus cold storage. Int Ophthalmol. 2008;28(3):155-163. doi:10.1007/s10792-007-9086-1
references.usedFor: Hypothermic storage at 2–6 °C (applied period 7–10 days for Optisol, claimed maximum 14–16 days; earlier M–K medium 2–3 days; death-to-storage usually ≤12 h); organ culture at 31–37 °C up to 4–5 weeks (death-to-storage 24–48 h; endothelial inspection after storage; detects contamination); moist chamber for whole globes; corneas cannot reliably be frozen; similar graft survival.

references.citation: Jahnukainen T, Lauronen J, Raissadati A, et al. Development of Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) Antibodies Against Vascular Homograft Donor in Pediatric Heart Transplant Recipients. Ann Transplant. 2019;24:454-460. doi:10.12659/aot.917232
references.usedFor: 12 paediatric heart transplant recipients with homografts: 67% HLA antibodies before transplant; after transplant 40% DSA against homograft donor; homograft-donor DSA first detected 13.6 years after insertion (one patient); grafts selected by ABO only, no immunosuppression; 40–60% of children develop HLA antibodies after allograft implantation (earlier studies); cryopreserved grafts contain viable endothelial cells; decellularisation reduces sensitisation.

references.citation: Huyan Y, Chang Y, Song J. Application of Homograft Valved Conduit in Cardiac Surgery. Front Cardiovasc Med. 2021;8:740871. doi:10.3389/fcvm.2021.740871
references.usedFor: Cryopreservation retains biological activity and some antigenicity; most recipients have humoral immunity against HLA; donor dendritic and endothelial cells expressing HLA class II; immune response related to early degeneration; antigenicity may lead to rejection and early calcification especially in children; matching ABO and HLA described as a research direction; decellularisation reduces immune response.

references.citation: Baskett RJ, Nanton MA, Warren AE, Ross DB. Human leukocyte antigen-DR and ABO mismatch are associated with accelerated homograft valve failure in children: implications for therapeutic interventions. J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg. 2003;126(1):232-239. doi:10.1016/s0022-5223(03)00210-1
references.usedFor: Abstract only (Europe PMC record; no open full text). 96 RVOT homografts in 83 children: younger age, ABO mismatch and (in the HLA-typed subgroup) HLA-DR mismatch associated with echocardiographic valve failure.

claims.text: Corneal immune privilege: no blood or lymphatic vessels, few mature APCs, FasL/PD-L1, aqueous humour, ACAID; no routine HLA typing.
Neovascularisation, regraft, inflammation and raised IOP lower survival; registry figures; high-risk rejection 30–60%; 20–30% rejection within 5 years overall.
FANCY (mixed normal- and high-risk patients): no significant benefit of HLA matching (15.7% vs 17%), underpowered; efficacy in high-risk grafts undetermined; some European centres match.
Hypothermic 2–6 °C, typically 7–10 days; organ culture 31–37 °C up to 4–5 weeks; death-to-storage times; corneas cannot reliably be frozen.

Valve homografts usually implanted without HLA matching or immunosuppression (both research directions); living HLA-bearing donor cells; most recipients make HLA antibodies; immune response linked to early degeneration; ABO and HLA-DR mismatch associated with faster failure in children.

Homograft recipients listed for heart transplant: 67% HLA antibodies; 40% DSA vs homograft donor after transplant; homograft-donor antibodies first detected 13.6 years after insertion in one patient; decellularisation reduces sensitisation.

Corneal enucleation within 6 h of death, transplant within 48–72 h; >90% long-term success and ~10% rejection; ABO matching not needed for corneas; valves function through nonviable connective tissue.
claims.note: Not taught as stated. Storage timings are outdated per Pels 2008; rejection figures are qualified by Böhringer 2018 and Armitage 2019; Huyan 2021 and Jahnukainen 2019 describe viable cells in cryopreserved valves; corneal ABO matching was not addressed in the sources read.

claims.text: Scenario invented; cornea and valve drawings schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 2 and Trap 1 say valve allografts need no ABO/HLA matching because they rely on nonviable connective tissue. Sources show cryopreserved homografts keep living HLA-bearing cells, that the immune response is linked to early degeneration, and that ABO and HLA-DR mismatch were associated with faster failure in children (Baskett 2003, abstract). The lesson teaches that valves are implanted without routine matching but are antigenic.

Hit 3 gives enucleation within 6 h, 4 °C storage and transplant within 48–72 h. Pels 2008 describes cold storage typically used for 7–10 days (claimed maximum 14–16), organ culture up to 4–5 weeks, and death-to-storage of ≤12 h (cold) or 24–48 h (organ culture). The lesson teaches the source.

Hit 3 gives ~10% rejection, mostly from vascularization, and >90% long-term success. Böhringer 2018 reports 20–30% with at least one rejection within 5 years; Armitage 2019 lists neovascularisation, regraft, inflammation and raised IOP as risk factors and 30–60% rejection in high-risk eyes. The lesson teaches the sources.

Trap 2 says high-risk corneal grafts do not need HLA matching (FANCY). FANCY enrolled both normal- and high-risk indications, found no significant benefit, and was underpowered; Armitage 2019 calls efficacy undetermined and notes some European centres still match. Practice is centre-dependent.
